clinicalPearls: Placental insufficiency describes inadequate placental transfer of oxygen and nutrients, most often manifesting as fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and, if progressive, fetal hypoxia
It commonly underlies placenta-mediated disease, linking fetal growth restriction with pre-eclampsia through the shared mechanism of deficient spiral artery remodelling

Risk factors include hypertensive disorders, maternal vascular and autoimmune disease such as antiphospholipid syndrome, pre-existing diabetes or renal disease, smoking, thrombophilia, and a previous growth-restricted or stillborn pregnancy

Distinguishing a constitutionally small but healthy fetus from a growth-restricted fetus with placental dysfunction is central and rests on growth trajectory and Doppler studies rather than size alone
Umbilical artery Doppler is the key surveillance tool: rising resistance, then absent, and finally reversed end-diastolic flow indicate worsening placental function and impending fetal compromise
In late-onset disease the cerebroplacental ratio and middle cerebral artery Doppler ('brain-sparing') may reveal redistribution even when the umbilical artery Doppler appears near-normal
Ductus venosus Doppler and computerised cardiotocography help time delivery in early-onset severe cases, where prematurity must be balanced against the risk of stillbirth
Management centres on surveillance and optimally timed delivery, with antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection when very preterm birth is planned
reference.pathophysiology: In normal pregnancy, extravillous trophoblast invades and remodels the maternal spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels that deliver a high, steady blood flow to the intervillous space. In placental insufficiency this transformation is incomplete, leaving high-resistance vessels prone to spasm and thrombosis; the resulting malperfusion causes placental ischaemia, infarction, and villous maldevelopment. Reduced surface area and impaired diffusion limit oxygen and nutrient transfer, restricting fetal growth. The fetus adapts by redistributing cardiac output to preserve the brain, heart, and adrenals at the expense of the kidneys and periphery, which reduces renal perfusion and amniotic fluid, producing oligohydramnios. Progressive hypoxaemia and acidaemia are reflected in deteriorating arterial and then venous Doppler indices and, ultimately, in abnormal cardiotocography and stillbirth if delivery is not achieved.
additionalDifferentials: A constitutionally small-for-gestational-age but healthy fetus
Fetal aneuploidy or a genetic syndrome causing growth restriction
Congenital infection such as cytomegalovirus or toxoplasmosis
Multiple pregnancy with twin-to-twin transfusion or selective growth restriction
Oligohydramnios from ruptured membranes or a fetal renal anomaly
additionalInvestigations: Serial ultrasound biometry to assess fetal size and growth velocity
Amniotic fluid volume assessment by deepest vertical pocket or amniotic fluid index
Umbilical artery Doppler for placental resistance and end-diastolic flow
Middle cerebral artery Doppler and cerebroplacental ratio for redistribution
Ductus venosus Doppler in early-onset severe restriction to help time delivery
Cardiotocography, including computerised analysis of short-term variation

Investigations for an underlying cause, including maternal blood pressure and urinalysis, uterine artery Doppler, screening for infection, thrombophilia or autoimmune disease, and karyotype or anomaly assessment where indicated
redFlags: Absent or reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow
Abnormal ductus venosus Doppler with an absent or reversed a-wave
Static or declining fetal growth on serial scans
Abnormal cardiotocography or reduced short-term variation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the severity and gestation at onset; late-onset, well-surveilled disease often does well with timely delivery, whereas early-onset severe insufficiency carries high risks of stillbirth, iatrogenic prematurity, and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.
pitfalls: Equating small fetal size with growth restriction, or vice versa, without Doppler and growth-trajectory assessment
Over-relying on a single normal umbilical artery Doppler in late-onset disease and missing redistribution
Failing to investigate for underlying maternal or fetal causes
Delivering too early or too late by not integrating the full surveillance picture
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on the small-for-gestational-age fetus
ISUOG practice guidelines on Doppler assessment and fetal growth
management: Intensive foetal surveillance with serial growth biometry, umbilical artery and ductus venosus Doppler and cardiotocography
Timing of delivery according to Doppler and cardiotocographic deterioration as the definitive intervention
Antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity ahead of anticipated preterm delivery
Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection when very preterm delivery is planned
Optimisation of underlying maternal disease such as hypertension, diabetes or antiphospholipid syndrome with aspirin and heparin
Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy in women at high risk of placental disease
Smoking cessation and modification of contributory factors
Delivery and neonatal care in a unit with an appropriate level of neonatal support
